body: The brush is loaded and he does not put it down, because the song has another minute left in it and he would like to hear the end of it. A man of about fifty is painting the outside of a windowsill on a Saturday, with the window pushed up as far as it goes and a radio balanced on the sill inside. When the song ends he does what everybody does now — wipes his hand down his jeans and picks up the phone to find out who that was. What comes back is not a name he knows. It is a twelve-character code, a chapter and verse out of a psalm, and a station he has never heard of. He looks at it a moment, then puts the phone back on the sill and reloads the brush.

That question is the one everybody asks about music made this way. It is fair, usually asked in good faith, and it almost always gets a slogan back instead of an answer. Here is the answer, and it is a chain rather than a name.

Take a single track on this band and follow it back. Before there was any audio there was a passage, chosen by somebody who wanted a specific thing said, and then a brief — what this song is for, who is likely to hear it, and what it must not claim.

It is worth slowing down on the word wrote, because it has done a great deal of quiet work for several centuries. A hymn most of a congregation can sing without the book will have a text by one person, a tune by somebody who never met them, a harmonisation by a third and an arrangement by a fourth whose name appears nowhere. The organist chooses the registration. The engineer decides what the room sounds like. Ask who wrote it and you are not asking who did the labour; you are asking whose judgement is in it, and who would answer for it if it said something false. That question has always had an answer. It has almost never been a single name.

Generation comes next, and it is the least interesting step in the chain: a model composes and performs against that brief. What comes back is read before anything else happens to it, and what survives is given a permanent twelve-character SongID — the identifier it carries onto every one of the 121 frequencies on this dial.

The reading is where the cost sits. A track is read for three things: whether it says what the passage says, whether the language is true, and whether it is any good. Those are three different questions, and a song can fail one while passing the others — a lovely arrangement of a sentiment that is not in the chapter, or a doctrinally exact lyric nobody would sing twice. A great many are discarded. Nothing goes on air unread, which is an expensive habit when reading is slow and generating is not. Every step that required a decision was made by a person. Every step that required labour was not.

Notice how selectively the anxiety about this operates. Most people who sang four songs in church last Sunday could not name the writer of one, or say which was assembled by a committee off a chord progression that tested well. The credits went quiet long before any model turned up. What changed is not that authorship became murky. It is that it became audible, and a murkiness you can hear is harder to live with than one you had stopped looking at.

So the chain is kept in the open, and attached to the identifier rather than to the title, which is what makes it checkable. A track cannot be quietly re-titled into something vaguer, re-credited to somebody more marketable, or swapped for a similar recording that says something slightly different, because the schedule and the play log both know it by its SongID. Ask what played at a quarter past four on a given frequency and there is an answer, and it is the same answer tomorrow.
None of which settles the objection. The objection was never really about paperwork.

The strongest version of it runs like this. A song is a testimony; a testimony has to have cost somebody something; and a machine has not sat up with a sick child, or buried anyone, or held a promise for eleven years without seeing it. That is not a silly thing to say — it is very nearly right, and the people who say it care most about the songs. But look at what the objection protects. The session singer on a worship record half the country knows was booked for the morning, handed a lyric she had not read, sang it eleven times and went to her next booking. Nobody has ever asked whether she meant it.
A machine can carry a sentence. It cannot mean one. Which is precisely why a person decides what it is given to carry.

A woman who has run the music at a small church for nineteen years is at her kitchen table on a Tuesday night with a mug going cold beside her, working out whether she can put a new song in front of about forty people on Sunday. The tune is not the problem. The second verse is, because she has been caught out before by a line that meant rather less than it sounded like it meant, and she was the one at the front when it did. She finds the passage listed under the track and reads the whole chapter, which takes four minutes. Then she prints the words out and puts them in her bag for the morning.
Nobody had to be trusted for that, and nobody had to be persuaded of anything. She could check, on a Tuesday, at her own table. That is the only thing a credit chain has ever been for.

Something real is lost here, and it should be said plainly rather than hedged. There is no room full of musicians behind these tracks, no story about the night it was written in a rented house at two in the morning, no argument about the bridge, no person you could write to and thank. And a share of the catalogue is simply ordinary — true, competent, unremarkable — in a way a band who had waited nine years for their one record would not have tolerated.

That loss is real, and it is not the thing that decides whether a song is worth singing. Most hymns that outlived their own centuries outlived their stories too. Hardly anybody who sings them knows what was happening in the writer’s life that year, and it makes no difference to what the words do at a graveside. The stories were ours to enjoy afterwards; they were never the warrant. What a song is asked, when somebody is leaning on it, is whether it is true.

So the honest answer to the man in the car park is not a name, and it is not a shrug either. A passage was chosen. A brief was written. What came back was read three ways and most of it was thrown out. A frequency was assigned and the schedule published before it aired. Every step that required a decision was made by a person, and every step that required labour was not — close to the arrangement a session-band hymn has always had. The labour has moved. The decisions have not.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 assigned frequencies, of which 46 are live at this moment. What is on them comes in four kinds. There is music, which is most of the band — worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened rather than sung. There is family programming, simply safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are 40 international frequencies carrying 29 languages besides English, hosted in those languages rather than translated into them. Every track on all of them came down the same chain.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 303.10 — Yes and Amen. It is the station where the chain this article has described is shortest and hardest to hide: the SingItDone declaration albums, all twelve of the Inspire Family, one record each, every song a first-person statement of what is already true of a believer rather than a request for it to become so. The station is named for the sentence it stands on — every promise of Elohim is Yes and Amen in Him. Because those songs declare rather than describe, the question gets sharp quickly. Somebody had to decide that a person may say this about themselves, out loud, and mean it. Put it on and what you are hearing is the decisions.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — the site is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets decided.

So take this as an invitation rather than a defence. You do not have to settle the authorship question before you are allowed to listen, and nobody ever settled it for a hymnbook either. Put HM 303.10 on this afternoon while you are doing something else, and let it run. If a line goes past that you want to argue with, read the chapter underneath it — that is what it is there for. And if one goes past that you catch yourself singing at the sink a fortnight later, you can find out exactly what it stood on.
